title: Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis
subject: Medicine
summary: SBP is an infection of ascitic fluid without an intra‑abdominal source, most common in cirrhosis. Diagnosis relies on ascitic neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³ and clinical suspicion. Prompt antibiotics and albumin improve survival.

sections.p: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis occurs when bacteria translocate from the gut lumen into ascitic fluid, usually in patients with decompensated cirrhosis. It presents with fever, abdominal pain or tenderness, and worsening encephalopathy, but may be subtle in low‑resource settings.
b: Most common in cirrhosis with ascites
Precipitating factors: GI bleed, recent antibiotics, HIV, TB, malaria

sections.p: Gram‑negative enteric bacilli (E. coli, Klebsiella) cause ~70 % of cases; gram‑positive cocci (Streptococcus, Enterococcus) account for the rest. Anaerobes are rare but reported in some African series.
b: Enteric bacteria dominate because of increased gut permeability
Antibiotic resistance patterns may reflect local HIV/TB drug use

sections.p: No external transmission; bacteria cross the intestinal mucosa (bacterial translocation) facilitated by portal hypertension, low protein in ascitic fluid, and immune dysfunction.
b: Portal hypertension → intestinal edema → bacterial overgrowth
Low ascitic complement and opsonins impair clearance

sections.p: Infection of sterile ascitic fluid leads to peritoneal inflammation, systemic sepsis, renal dysfunction (hepatorenal syndrome), and can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.
b: Acute kidney injury is the leading cause of early death
Progressive encephalopathy may mask abdominal signs

sections.p: Diagnosis rests on paracentesis with cell count and culture. In low‑resource hospitals, bedside microscopy and rapid Gram stain guide early therapy when culture facilities are absent.

t.b: Is SBP present? – ≥250 cells/mm³ confirms infection
What organism is likely? – Presence of Gram‑negative rods suggests enteric bacteria; guides empiric choice
Is ascites portal‑hypertensive? – SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL supports cirrhotic ascites, the typical setting for SBP
Is renal dysfunction developing? – Rising creatinine signals hepatorenal syndrome, prompting albumin

sections.p: Start empiric third‑generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefotaxime) immediately after paracentesis, plus intravenous albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 to prevent renal failure. Adjust antibiotics when culture results return.
b: Cefotaxime chosen for broad Gram‑negative coverage and low nephrotoxicity
Avoid aminoglycosides in cirrhosis because of renal risk
If cephalosporin unavailable, use ampicillin‑sulbactam if local resistance is low

sections.p: Key bedside steps: (1) suspect SBP in any cirrhotic patient with new fever, pain or encephalopathy; (2) perform urgent paracentesis; (3) start antibiotics before results; (4) give albumin if creatinine rises or baseline >1 mg/dL; (5) monitor for renal failure and encephalopathy.
b: Paracentesis is safe even in coagulopathy; delay increases mortality
A neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³ is diagnostic regardless of culture
Prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., norfloxacin) after an episode reduce recurrence

whenToSeekHelp: Septic shock (hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status)

faq.a: Rarely; it can be seen in nephrotic syndrome or peritoneal dialysis, but cirrhosis accounts for >90 % of cases.

faq.q: Why is albumin given with antibiotics?
faq.a: Albumin expands intravascular volume, improves renal perfusion, and reduces the risk of hepatorenal syndrome.

faq.q: What if the ascitic fluid culture is negative?
faq.a: A neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³ still confirms SBP; treat empirically.

exam: A cirrhotic patient presents with fever and mild abdominal tenderness – what is your immediate next step? — Perform diagnostic paracentesis before any imaging.
Ascitic fluid shows 300 cells/mm³ neutrophils, Gram stain negative – how do you interpret this? — Meets SBP criteria; start empiric antibiotics despite negative stain.
Why is cefotaxime preferred over ciprofloxacin for initial SBP therapy? — Better Gram‑negative coverage, lower resistance, and safer in renal impairment.
A patient on prophylactic norfloxacin develops SBP – what does this indicate about the organism? — Likely resistant gram‑positive or atypical organism; modify antibiotics based on culture.
How does bacterial translocation lead to SBP in portal hypertension? — Increased intestinal permeability, bacterial overgrowth, and impaired immune clearance allow organisms to enter ascitic fluid.
What are the indications for giving albumin in SBP? — Serum creatinine >1 mg/dL or BUN >30 mg/dL, or development of hepatorenal syndrome.

Differentiate SBP from tuberculous peritonitis in a low‑resource setting. — SBP: acute fever, neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³, rapid response to antibiotics; TB: subacute, lymphocyte‑predominant ascites, low neutrophils, poor response to cephalosporins.
What are the key warning signs that require urgent transfer to a higher‑level facility? — Septic shock, rapidly rising creatinine, refractory encephalopathy, massive hemorrhage.
